title: Jeremiah 27:12–22
context: Jeremiah speaks to Zedekiah king of Judah with the same words: bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, serve him and his people, and live. Why die by sword, famine, and pestilence? The prophets who say Judah shall not serve are not to be heard; the LORD has not sent them, and they prophesy falsely in his name. Jeremiah also speaks to the priests and to all the people: they are not to listen to those who say the vessels of the LORD’s house will shortly be brought again from Babylon. If those prophets are sent, let them intercede that the vessels still left in the temple, in the king’s house, and at Jerusalem may not go to Babylon. Concerning the pillars, the sea, the bases, and the rest of the vessels left after Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah and the nobles away, the LORD says those remaining things will be carried to Babylon and will be there until the day he visits them; then he will bring them up and restore them to this place. The yoke is still the plain call to serve Babylon and live. Jeconiah’s being carried away is also told in 2 Kings 24, and the later fall in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52; those accounts should be named without being blended here. Identities and dates around that first carrying-away may be hedged.

verses.text: I spoke to Zedekiah king of Judah according to all these words, saying, “Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I spoke to Zedekiah king of Judah according to all these words, saying, “Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live.” Jeremiah now addresses Zedekiah with the same charge already sent to the neighboring kings. The yoke is plain: serve and live. The speaker of the report is Jeremiah; the charge is the word he has been given.

Arminian readers hear a real appeal to the king, a path of life still set before him if he will bring his neck under the yoke, not a sentence already closed against Judah’s last king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same address as the LORD’s word in Jeremiah’s mouth to Zedekiah: serve Babylon and live. The call is as serious as the warning that follows.

Shared ground: Zedekiah is told to submit and live. The verse does not narrate whether he will, and later chapters should not be read back as if this appeal had not been made.

verses.text: Why will you die, you and your people, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why will you die, you and your people, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?” The question presses the cost of refusal. Death by the three blows already named would fall on the king and on the people together.

Arminian readers take the “Why will you die” as a genuine plea. The death is not presented as unavoidable in this line; it is the end of the path of not serving, a path they are urged to leave.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same question as the LORD’s already spoken word applied to Zedekiah and the people: the nation that will not serve will die by those three means.

Shared ground: sword, famine, and pestilence remain the stated alternative to service. The question is not a riddle.

verses.text: Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who speak to you, saying, ‘You shall not serve the king of Babylon;’ for they prophesy a lie to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who speak to you, saying, ‘You shall not serve the king of Babylon;’ for they prophesy a lie to you.” The same lie already forbidden to the foreign courts is now forbidden in Jerusalem. The quoted promise is short and clear, and it is called a lie.

Arminian readers hear a warning Judah can still obey: these prophets are not to be followed, even when their word is the word a king would rather hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the prohibition as the LORD’s, through Jeremiah: the word “You shall not serve the king of Babylon” is a lie, and it is not to be heard.

Shared ground: the conflict is over this specific promise, not a general theory of prophecy invented for the passage. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named later by reference; it need not be restated as a new contrast here.

verses.text: For I have not sent them,” says the LORD, “but they prophesy falsely in my name; that I may drive you out, and that you may perish, you, and the prophets who prophesy to you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For I have not sent them,” says the LORD, “but they prophesy falsely in my name; that I may drive you out, and that you may perish, you, and the prophets who prophesy to you.” The LORD denies that he has sent these prophets. They use his name, and the end of that false word would be driving out and perishing, for the hearers and for the prophets themselves.

Arminian readers take “I have not sent them” as a real verdict on this message, and the warning as one Judah can still heed, so as not to perish with those prophets.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same unsent status as the LORD’s own word: they prophesy falsely in his name, and driving out and perishing would follow for people and prophets together.

Shared ground: they are not sent, and the false word is deadly. The verse is a charge, not a new party contrast over prophecy.

verses.text: Also I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, the LORD says, “Don’t listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Behold, the vessels of the LORD’s house will now shortly be brought again from Babylon;’ for they prophesy a lie to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah also spoke “to the priests and to all this people,” with the LORD’s word: “Don’t listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Behold, the vessels of the LORD’s house will now shortly be brought again from Babylon;’ for they prophesy a lie to you.” A second form of the lie is a soon return of the temple vessels. The priests, who care for those vessels, are addressed directly.

Arminian readers hear a specific false hope: a short time, and the vessels home again. That hope is called a lie, and the priests and people can refuse it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same saying as a lie the LORD forbids. The vessels will not “now shortly” come back, whatever prophets promise the priests.

Shared ground: the timing “now shortly” is the heart of this deception. A later restoration, named at the end of the unit, is not the same as this near return.

verses.text: Don’t listen to them. Serve the king of Babylon, and live. Why should this city become a desolation?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t listen to them. Serve the king of Babylon, and live. Why should this city become a desolation?” The charge is repeated in three strokes: do not listen, serve, and live. The city’s becoming a desolation is the alternative held up before them.

Arminian readers take “Why should this city become a desolation?” as a real question, an appeal that Jerusalem’s ruin is not yet the only path if they will serve and live.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same short commands as the LORD’s word for the city’s life: serve the king of Babylon, and live, rather than let the city become a desolation.

Shared ground: listening to the lying prophets and refusing the yoke is the way toward desolation. The city is still being warned.

verses.text: But if they are prophets, and if the LORD’s word is with them, let them now make intercession to the LORD of Armies, that the vessels which are left in the LORD’s house, in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem, don’t go to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But if they are prophets, and if the LORD’s word is with them, let them now make intercession to the LORD of Armies, that the vessels which are left in the LORD’s house, in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem, don’t go to Babylon.” The test proposed is prayer, not a new slogan of return. If the LORD’s word is with them, let them intercede that the remaining vessels not go.

Arminian readers hear a searching test: true standing would show itself in intercession for what is still left, a prayer they might actually make, rather than in promises of a short return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “if” as a challenge to those prophets. If the LORD’s word is with them, they should intercede now that the remaining vessels not go to Babylon.

Shared ground: intercession for what is left is set over against the lie of a soon return. The verse does not need a new contrast over prayer.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies says concerning the pillars, concerning the sea, concerning the bases, and concerning the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the LORD of Armies says concerning the pillars, concerning the sea, concerning the bases, and concerning the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,” The list is of what still remains: pillars, sea, bases, and other vessels, after an earlier carrying-away. The sentence continues into the next verses and should not be closed sooner than the text closes it.

Arminian readers take the inventory as a sober account of what is still in Jerusalem, the very things the false word would treat as already safe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a word about specific remaining furniture of the house and the city, named so that the following promise and warning have a clear object.

Shared ground: some vessels are still left. Their future is the LORD’s to announce, not the prophets’ to shorten.

verses.text: which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon didn’t take when he carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem to Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem—
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the vessels “which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon didn’t take when he carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem to Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem—” An earlier deportation is assumed, of Jeconiah, the nobles, and some vessels; these remaining things were not taken then. 2 Kings 24 tells of that stage of the exile; the accounts should be named without being blended, and the dates and identifications around Jeconiah may be hedged. Jeconiah is often identified with the Jehoiachin of that narrative, a common reading that need not be pressed as a proof here.

Arminian readers take the verse as historical setting for the remaining vessels, a real prior carrying-away, not a vague backdrop.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise rest the “vessels that are left” on that earlier captivity of Jeconiah and the nobles, which 2 Kings 24 and later chapters also know, without forcing a single combined chronology in this note.

Shared ground: not everything was taken when Jeconiah was carried away. What was left is still in danger of going.

verses.text: yes, the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning the vessels that are left in the LORD’s house, and in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem:
verses.arminianNotes:
“yes, the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning the vessels that are left in the LORD’s house, and in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem:” The remaining vessels in temple, palace, and city are again the subject. The line is an opening to the verdict of the next verse.

Arminian readers hear the repetition as weight: the God of Israel is about to speak specifically of what is left, not of a general rumor about all the furniture of the first carrying-away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same heading as the LORD’s formal word about the leftover vessels in the three locations already named.

Shared ground: the subject is the vessels still in Jerusalem. Their fate is not in the lying prophets’ mouths.

verses.text: ‘They will be carried to Babylon, and there they will be, until the day that I visit them,’ says the LORD; ‘then I will bring them up, and restore them to this place.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will be carried to Babylon, and there they will be, until the day that I visit them,” says the LORD; “then I will bring them up, and restore them to this place.” The remaining vessels will go, will stay, and will in time be restored, when the LORD visits them. That later bringing-up is not the “now shortly” of verse 16. How this visit relates to the seventy years of 29:10, or to Daniel 9:2, 2 Chronicles 36:21, and Ezra 1:1, may be named later by reference and should not be turned into one scheme here.

Arminian readers hear both judgment and a real later restoration of the vessels. The hope is dated to the LORD’s visiting, not to the short timetable the false prophets offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sequence as the LORD’s: carried, remaining in Babylon until he visits, then brought up and restored to this place.

Shared ground: the vessels will go, and they will in time come home, on the LORD’s day of visiting, not on the prophets’ short schedule.
